0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 3.0pt\raise-2.5pt\hbox{$\textstyle{\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\hat{\Lambda}{\textup{-Mod}}_{\textup{Fd}}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}$}}}}}}}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces{}{\hbox{\lx@xy@droprule}}\ignorespaces{\hbox{\kern 32.25078pt\raise-2.15277pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\lx@xy@tip{1}\lx@xy@tip{-1}}}}}}{\hbox{\lx@xy@droprule}}{\hbox{\lx@xy@droprule}}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces{}{\hbox{\lx@xy@droprule}}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces{\hbox{\kern 132.09166pt\raise 2.15277pt\hbox{{}\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 3.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{$\scriptstyle{}$}}}\kern 3.0pt}}}}}}\ignorespaces{\hbox{\kern 149.21616pt\raise 2.15277pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\lx@xy@tip{1}\lx@xy@tip{-1}}}}}}{\hbox{\lx@xy@droprule}}{\hbox{\lx@xy@droprule}}{\hbox{\kern 149.21616pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 3.0pt\raise-2.5pt\hbox{$\textstyle{\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces H^{0}(\textup{Tw}^{0}\mathcal{A}_{F})}$}}}}}}}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces{}{\hbox{\lx@xy@droprule}}\ignorespaces{\hbox{\kern 113.21616pt\raise-2.15277pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\lx@xy@tip{1}\lx@xy@tip{-1}}}}}}{\hbox{\lx@xy@droprule}}{\hbox{\lx@xy@droprule}}\ignorespaces}}}}\ignorespaces\ .

Proof.

The mutually inverse equivalences on the left of each diagram have already been established in Theorem
3.20
, following Bridgeland
[
Bri02
]
and Van den Bergh
[
Ber04b
]
. The equivalences on the right follow from the identifications

\Lambda{\textup{-Mod}}_{\textup{fd}}\cong\textup{filt}(S_{i})\xrightarrow{\cong}\textup{filt}(\Sigma_{i})\cong H^{0}(\textup{tw}^{0}\mathcal{A}_{F})\ ,

and similarly in the ungraded case

\Lambda{\textup{-Mod}}_{\textup{Fd}}\cong\textup{Filt}(S_{i})\xrightarrow{\cong}\textup{Filt}(\Sigma_{i})\cong H^{0}(\textup{Tw}^{0}\mathcal{A}_{F})\ ,

where the first isomorphism in each line follows from the existence of Jordan-Holder filtrations, as in the proof of Proposition
3.6
for example, and the final isomorphism in each line follows from Corollaries
2.57
and
2.48
, respectively. Finally, the middle equivalence in each line follows from the fact that triangulated functors preserve categories of iterated extensions, and we have seen that the given functor maps
S_{i}
to
\Sigma_{i}
(and, in the graded case, preserves grading shifts in the unsheared conventions).
∎

We note that this equivalence is indeed a generalization of Theorem
3.20
, in the sense that we have the following proposition:

Proposition 3.28
.

Suppose
\Lambda
is a Koszul algebra. Then the cohomological grading shear equivalence of Remark
2.30
restricts to an equivalence of mixed categories

H^{0}(\textup{tw}^{0}\mathcal{A}_{F})\xrightarrow{\cong}\textup{LCP}(\Sigma)\ .

Proof.

For
\Lambda
a Koszul algebra, the corresponding Koszul dual algebra
\Sigma
is a plain, Koszul associative algebra, and thus the
A_{\infty}
bimodule structure maps

\rho^{\Sigma_{i_{1},...,i_{d}}}_{t,k}:\Sigma^{\otimes t}\otimes\Sigma_{i_{1},...,i_{d}}\otimes\mathcal{E}_{\Sigma}^{\otimes k}\to\Sigma_{i_{1},...,i_{d}}[1-t-k]

of Equation
2.14
necessarily vanish for
t\geq 2
,
k\geq 2
and for
t=k=1
and
t=k=0
. Thus, the only non-trivial structure maps for objects in
H^{0}(\textup{tw}^{0}\mathcal{A}_{F})
are
\rho_{1,0}
and
\rho_{0,1}
. The former is simply the usual
\Sigma
module structure map on the direct sum of projective modules
\Sigma_{i_{1},...,i_{d}}
, and the latter gives precisely the usual allowed linear differentials defining a linear complex of projectives.
∎

Next, we describe the analogous monad formalism arising from Theorem
3.27
, generalizing Proposition
3.26
to the
A_{\infty}
case. Given an object
(i_{1},...,i_{d},\delta)\in\textup{tw}^{0}\mathcal{A}_{F}
, the corresponding object of
{\textup{D}}_{\textup{fd}}(\Sigma)
has underlying bigraded vector space given by

\Sigma_{i_{1},...,i_{d}}=\bigoplus_{k=1,...,d}\Sigma_{i_{k}}\langle p_{k}\rangle\cong\bigoplus_{i\in I}\Sigma_{i}\otimes V_{i}

where each
V_{i}
is a graded vector space

V_{i}=\bigoplus_{p\in\mathbb{Z}}V_{i,-p}\langle p\rangle\quad\quad\text{with}\quad\quad\dim V_{i,p}=\#\{k\in\{1,...,d\}\ |\ i_{k}=i\textup{ and }p_{k}=p\}\ .

Note in particular that
\dim\oplus_{i\in I}V_{i}=d
.

Now, the degree zero element
\delta\in\mathfrak{gl}_{r}(\mathbb{Z}\mathcal{A}_{F})[1]
is in fact an element of the subspace

\delta\in\Hom_{{\textup{D}}(\Sigma)}(\bigoplus_{i\in I}\Sigma_{i}\otimes V_{i},\bigoplus_{j\in I}\Sigma_{j}\otimes V_{j}[1])\subset\mathfrak{gl}_{d}(\Sigma)[1]\cong\mathfrak{gl}_{d}(\mathcal{A}_{F})[1]

and thus admits a decomposition

(3.31)

\delta=\sum_{i,j\in I}b_{ij}\otimes B_{ij}\quad\in\quad\bigoplus_{i,j\in I}\ {}_{i}\Sigma_{j}\otimes\Hom(V_{i},V_{j})[1]\ ,

as in Equation
3.27
, where we again use the abuse of notation
B_{ij}\otimes b_{ij}
to denote the not necessarily pure tensor, as in Warning
3.25
.

The
A_{\infty}
module structure maps for
\Sigma_{i_{1},...,i_{d}}^{\delta}
are corrected from those of
\Sigma_{i_{1},...,i_{d}}
, the underlying direct sum of rank 1 free modules, by the higher
(\mathcal{A}_{F},\mathcal{E}_{\mathcal{A}_{F}})
bimodule structure maps evaluated on the tensor powers of
\delta
, according to Equation
2.17
. In particular, the underlying cochain complex differential is given by

d_{\delta}=\sum_{k\in\mathbb{Z}}\rho_{k}^{\Sigma}(\cdot,\delta^{\otimes k-1})\quad\in\quad\Hom_{{\textup{D}}(\Sigma)}(\Sigma_{i_{1},...,i_{d}},\Sigma_{i_{1},...,i_{d}}[1])

where
\rho_{k}^{\Sigma}:\Sigma_{i_{1},...,i_{d}}\otimes\Sigma^{\otimes k-1}\to\Sigma_{i_{1},...,i_{d}}[1-k]
denote the
A_{\infty}
module structure maps for
\Sigma_{i_{1},...,i_{d}}
over
\mathcal{E}_{\mathcal{A}_{F}}
. Decomposing according to Equation
3.31
, we have the analogous decomposition

(3.32)

d_{\delta}=\sum_{k\in\mathbb{Z},\ i,i_{2},...,i_{k-1},j\in I}m_{k}^{\Sigma}(\cdot,b_{ii_{2}},...,b_{i_{k-1}j})\otimes(B_{ii_{2}}...B_{i_{k-1}j})\quad\in\quad\bigoplus_{i,j\in I}\Hom(\Sigma_{i},\Sigma_{j}[1])\otimes\Hom(V_{i},V_{j})\

of the differential on
\Sigma_{i_{1},...,i_{d}}^{\delta}
. Thus, the image of the Nakayama dual of
\Sigma_{i_{1},...,i_{r}}^{\delta}\in{\textup{D}_{\textup{perf}}}(\Sigma)
under the Koszul duality equivalence of Equation
3.18
is given by

(3.33)

K(\Sigma_{i_{1},...,i_{d}}^{\delta,N})=\left(K(\Sigma_{i_{1},...,i_{d}}^{N}),K(d_{\delta}^{N})\right)\quad\quad\text{where}\quad\quad K(\Sigma_{i_{1},...,i_{d}}^{N})=\bigoplus_{i\in I}K(I_{i})\otimes V_{i}\ ,

and where the differential
K(d_{\delta}^{N}):K(\Sigma_{i_{1},...,i_{d}}^{N})\to K(\Sigma_{i_{1},...,i_{d}}^{N})[1]
is given by

(3.34)

\hskip-28.45274ptK(d_{\delta}^{N}):=\sum K(m_{k}^{\Sigma}(\cdot,b_{i,i_{2}},...,b_{i_{k-1},j})^{N})\otimes(B_{i,i_{2}}...B_{i_{k-2},j})\quad\in\quad\bigoplus_{i,j\in I}\Hom(K(I_{i}),K(I_{j})[1])\otimes\Hom(V_{i},V_{j})\ ,

where the sum is over the same index set as in Equation
3.32
above.

We also introduce the notation
d_{B}:\tilde{H}\to\tilde{H}[1]
, where
\tilde{H}\in\textup{PervCoh}_{\textup{cs}}(Y)^{\mathbb{C}^{\times}}
is as in Equation
3.28
for the map

(3.35)

d_{B}=\sum_{k\in\mathbb{Z},\ i,i_{2},...,i_{k-1},j\in I}K(m_{k}^{\Sigma}(\cdot,b_{i,i_{2}},...,b_{i_{k-1},j})^{N})\otimes(B_{i,i_{2}}...B_{i_{k-2},j})\ .

This is essentially the same as the map in Equation
3.34
above, but emphasizes that a differential of this functional form is determined uniquely by the choice of linear maps
B=(B_{i,j}^{\alpha})
, generalizing the definition of
d_{B}
in Equation
3.29
.

We can now state the desired generalization of Proposition
3.26
:

Proposition 3.29
.

Let
\tilde{H}\in\textup{PervCoh}_{\textup{cs}}(Y)^{T}
be as in Equation
3.28
and fix

B:=(B_{ij})_{i,j\in I}\quad\quad\text{with}\quad\quad B_{ij}=(B_{ij}^{\alpha}\in\Hom(V_{i},V_{j}))_{\alpha\in\mathcal{B}_{ij}}\ .

The following are equivalent:

•

the induced map
d_{B}:\tilde{H}\to\tilde{H}[1]
of Equation
3.35
satisfies
d_{B}^{2}=0
, and

•

the induced map
\rho:(\Sigma^{1})^{\vee}\to{\underline{\textup{End}}}_{S{\textup{-BiMod}}}(V)
of Equation
3.26
defines a representation of the graded DG quiver
Q_{Y}
.

Further, when these conditions hold, the resulting complex
(\tilde{H},d_{B})
is a projective resolution of the object
H\in\textup{PervCoh}_{\textup{cs}}(Y)^{T}
corresponding to the quiver representation
V\in\Lambda{\textup{-Mod}}_{\textup{fd}}
.

Similarly, for
\tilde{H}\in\textup{PervCoh}_{\textup{cs}}(\hat{Y})
as in Equation
3.28
, the following are equivalent:

•

the induced map
d_{B}:\tilde{H}\to\tilde{H}[1]
of Equation
3.35
satisfies
d_{B}^{2}=0
, and

•

the induced map
\rho:(\Sigma^{1})^{\vee}\to{\underline{\textup{End}}}_{S{\textup{-BiMod}}}(V)
of Equation
3.26
defines a nilpotent representation of the DG quiver
Q_{Y}
.

Further, when these conditions hold, the resulting complex
(\tilde{H},d_{B})
is a projective resolution of the object
H\in\textup{PervCoh}_{\textup{cs}}(\hat{Y})
corresponding to the quiver representation
V\in\Lambda{\textup{-Mod}}_{\textup{Fd}}
.

Proof.

By definition, the putative differential
d_{B}
is uniquely determined by an element
\delta
as in Equation
3.31
by the formula for
d_{\delta}
given in Equation
3.32
, and by the standard argument for
A_{\infty}
algebras the condition
d_{\delta}^{2}=0
is equivalent to the Maurer-Cartan equation for
\delta
of Equation
2.9
.

The Maurer-Cartan equation can be restated as a system of equations on the linear algebraic data
B_{ij}\in\Hom(V_{i},V_{j})
with coefficients determined by the higher products of the corresponding elements
b_{ij}\in\Sigma[1]
. Indeed, for
i,j\in I
, the corresponding component of the Maurer-Cartan equation on
\delta\in\mathfrak{gl}_{d}(\mathcal{A}_{F})
is given by

(3.36)

0=\left(\sum_{t\in\mathbb{N}}m_{t}(\delta^{\otimes t})\right)_{ij}=\sum_{t\in\mathbb{N}}\sum_{i_{2},...,i_{t-1}\in I}m_{t}(b_{ii_{2}},...,b_{i_{t-1}j})\otimes(B_{ii_{2}}\cdots B_{i_{t-1}j})\ ,

understood as a polynomial equation on the linear maps
B_{ij}
. Thus, we need to show that these equations are equivalent to the requirement that the collection of linear maps
B_{ij}
define a representation of the quiver
Q_{Y}
, or equivalently a module over the path algebra
\Lambda=\Sigma^{!}
.

The element
\delta
is equivalent to the map of
S
bimodules

\rho:(\Sigma^{1})^{\vee}\to{\underline{\textup{End}}}(V)

as in Equation
3.26
, and extends by the free-forgetful adjunction to define a map of algebras internal to
S{\textup{-BiMod}}

r_{\rho}:\Lambda^{0}=\otimes_{S}^{\bullet}(\Sigma^{1})^{\vee}\to{\underline{\textup{End}}}(V)\ .

The map
r_{\rho}
extends to define a module structure on
V
over the path algebra
\Lambda
of the DG quiver
Q_{Y}
if and only if the composition

\Lambda^{-1}\xrightarrow{d_{\Lambda}}\Lambda^{0}\xrightarrow{r_{\rho}}{\underline{\textup{End}}}(V)

vanishes. The differential
d_{\Lambda}
is defined on the generators

(\Sigma^{2})^{\vee}\subset\Lambda^{-1}=(\Sigma^{2})^{\vee}\otimes_{S}\otimes_{S}^{\bullet}(\Sigma^{1})^{\vee}

of
\Lambda^{-1}
over
\Lambda^{0}
, by the formula

d_{\Lambda}=\sum_{t\in\mathbb{N}}m_{t}^{\vee}:(\Sigma^{2})^{\vee}\to\otimes^{\bullet}_{S}(\Sigma^{1})^{\vee}\ ,

that is, as the sum of the duals of the
A_{\infty}
multiplication maps

m_{t}:\otimes^{t}_{S}\Sigma\to\Sigma[2-n]\ .

Thus, vanishing of the composition

r_{\rho}\circ d_{\Lambda}=r_{\rho}\circ\sum_{t\in\mathbb{N}}m_{t}^{\vee}=\sum_{t\in\mathbb{N}}\rho^{\otimes t}\circ m_{t}^{\vee}\ :(\Sigma^{2})^{\vee}\to{\underline{\textup{End}}}(V)

is equivalent under Hom-tensor adjunction to the vanishing of the element

\sum_{t\in\mathbb{N}}m_{t}(\delta^{\otimes t})=\sum_{t\in\mathbb{N}}\sum_{i_{1},...,i_{t}\in I}m_{n}(b_{i_{1}i_{2}},...,b_{i_{t-1}i_{t}})\otimes(B_{i_{1}i_{2}}\cdots B_{i_{t-1}i_{t}})\ \in\Sigma^{2}\otimes_{S}{\underline{\textup{End}}}(V)\ ,

which is evidently equivalent to the vanishing of the Maurer-Cartan equation given in Equation
3.36
, as desired.
∎

3.6.
Moduli spaces of perverse coherent sheaves and quivers with potential

In this section, we formulate and prove the first variant of Theorem
A
from the introduction. The categorical results discussed above determine a description of the moduli stacks of objects in the categories we have introduced above in terms of linear algebraic data. We begin by recalling the geometric description of the moduli stack of quiver representations and then state the main result establishing its equivalence with the moduli stack of perverse coherent sheaves.

Let
Q
be a graded quiver with edge set
E_{Q}
, vertex set
V_{Q}
, and path algebra

{\mathbb{K}}Q=\otimes^{\bullet}_{S}{\mathbb{K}}\langle E_{Q}\rangle\quad\quad\text{where}\quad\quad S=\oplus_{i\in V_{Q}}S_{i}=\oplus_{i\in V_{Q}}{\mathbb{K}}

as in Section
2.4
. For each dimension vector
{\textbf{d}}=(d_{i})\in\mathbb{N}^{V_{Q}}
, define

X_{\textbf{d}}(Q)=\bigoplus_{e\in E_{Q}}\Hom({\mathbb{K}}^{d_{s(e)}},{\mathbb{K}}^{d_{t(e)}})\quad\quad\textup{and}\quad\quad G_{\textbf{d}}(Q)=\prod_{i\in V_{Q}}{\textup{Gl}}_{d_{i}}({\mathbb{K}})\ .

The stack of representations
\mathfrak{M}(Q)
of
Q
is defined as the disjoint union of the quotient stacks

\mathfrak{M}(Q)=\bigsqcup_{{\textbf{d}}\in\mathbb{N}^{V_{Q}}}\mathfrak{M}_{\textbf{d}}(Q)\quad\quad\text{where}\quad\quad\mathfrak{M}_{\textbf{d}}(Q)=\left[X_{\textbf{d}}(Q)/G_{\textbf{d}}(Q)\right]\ .

Let
{\underline{\textup{End}}}({\mathbb{K}}^{\textbf{d}}):=\Hom({\mathbb{K}}^{\textbf{d}},{\mathbb{K}}^{\textbf{d}})\in S{\textup{-BiMod}}
denote the matrix algebra on
{\mathbb{K}}^{\textbf{d}}=\oplus_{i\in V_{Q}}{\mathbb{K}}^{d_{i}}
with its natural
S
bimodule structure, and note that there are canonical identifications

X_{\textbf{d}}(Q)\cong\Hom_{S{\textup{-BiMod}}}({\mathbb{K}}\langle E_{Q}\rangle,{\underline{\textup{End}}}({\mathbb{K}}^{\textbf{d}}))\cong\Hom_{\textup{Alg}_{\textup{Ass}}(S{\textup{-BiMod}})}({\mathbb{K}}Q,{\underline{\textup{End}}}({\mathbb{K}}^{\textbf{d}}))\ ,

so that we have

\mathfrak{M}_{\textbf{d}}(Q)({\mathbb{K}})\cong\{V\in S{\textup{-Mod}}_{\textup{fd}},\ \varphi\in\Hom_{\textup{Alg}_{\textup{Ass}}(S{\textup{-BiMod}})}({\mathbb{K}}Q,{\underline{\textup{End}}}(V))\ |\ \dim V={\textbf{d}}\ \}\ ,

that is, the groupoid of geometric points of
\mathfrak{M}_{\textbf{d}}
is the maximal subgroupoid of modules over the free path algebra
{\mathbb{K}}Q
of dimension
d
over
S
.

Now, suppose
(Q,R)
is a quiver with relations
R\subset{\mathbb{K}}Q
, as in Definition
2.22
, and define the closed subvariety
Z_{\textbf{d}}(Q,R)\subset X_{\textbf{d}}(Q)
by

Z_{\textbf{d}}(Q,R)=\{\varphi\in\Hom_{\textup{Alg}_{\textup{Ass}}(S{\textup{-BiMod}})}({\mathbb{K}}Q,{\underline{\textup{End}}}({\mathbb{K}}^{\textbf{d}}))\ |\ \varphi(R)=\{0\}\ \subset{\underline{\textup{End}}}({\mathbb{K}}^{\textbf{d}})\}\ .

Note that
Z_{\textbf{d}}(Q,R)
is
G_{\textbf{d}}(Q)
-invariant, as the condition that the corresponding map to
{\underline{\textup{End}}}_{S{\textup{-BiMod}}}(V)
satisfies
\varphi(R)=0
is well-defined, independent of the choice of isomorphism
V\cong{\mathbb{K}}^{\textbf{d}}
. The stack of representations
\mathfrak{M}(Q,R)
of
(Q,R)
is defined analogously as the disjoint union of the quotient stacks

\mathfrak{M}(Q,R)=\bigsqcup_{{\textbf{d}}\in\mathbb{N}^{V_{Q}}}\mathfrak{M}_{\textbf{d}}(Q,R)\quad\quad\textup{where}\quad\quad\mathfrak{M}_{\textbf{d}}(Q,R)=\left[Z_{\textbf{d}}(Q,R)/G_{\textbf{d}}(Q)\right]

and we have the analogous description of the geometric points

\mathfrak{M}_{\textbf{d}}(Q,R)({\mathbb{K}})=\{V\in S{\textup{-BiMod}},\ \varphi\in\Hom_{\textup{Alg}_{\textup{Ass}}(S{\textup{-BiMod}})}({\mathbb{K}}Q/R,{\underline{\textup{End}}}(V))\ |\ \dim V={\textbf{d}}\ \}

as parameterizing the modules over the path algebra
{\mathbb{K}}Q_{R}={\mathbb{K}}Q/R
of dimension
d
over
S
.

Finally, suppose
(Q,W)
is a quiver with potential
W\in{\mathbb{K}}Q_{\textup{cyc}}={\mathbb{K}}Q/[{\mathbb{K}}Q,{\mathbb{K}}Q]
, as in Definition
2.34
. Then we obtain a canonical function

\textup{Tr}(W)_{\textbf{d}}:X_{\textbf{d}}(Q)\to{\mathbb{K}}\quad\quad\textup{defined by}\quad\quad\varphi\mapsto\textup{Tr}_{{\mathbb{K}}^{\textbf{d}}}(\varphi(W))

where we identify
\varphi\in X_{\textbf{d}}(Q)\cong\Hom_{\textup{Alg}_{\textup{Ass}}(S{\textup{-BiMod}})}({\mathbb{K}}Q,{\underline{\textup{End}}}({\mathbb{K}}^{\textbf{d}}))
, and we define the closed subvariety
Z_{\textbf{d}}(Q,W)\subset X_{\textbf{d}}(Q)
by

Z_{\textbf{d}}(Q,W):=\textup{Crit}(\textup{Tr}(W)_{\textbf{d}})=\Gamma_{d\textup{Tr}(W)_{\textbf{d}}}\times_{T^{\vee}X_{\textbf{d}}}X_{\textbf{d}}\ .

Again,
Z_{\textbf{d}}(Q,W)
is
G_{\textbf{d}}
invariant, since the function
\textup{Tr}(W)_{\textbf{d}}
is itself, and the stack of representations of
(Q,W)
is defined as the disjoint union of the quotient stacks

\mathfrak{M}_{\textbf{d}}(Q,W)=\bigsqcup_{{\textbf{d}}\in\mathbb{N}^{V_{Q}}}\mathfrak{M}_{\textbf{d}}(Q,W)\quad\quad\textup{where}\quad\quad\mathfrak{M}_{\textbf{d}}(Q,W)=\left[Z_{\textbf{d}}(Q,W)/G_{\textbf{d}}(Q)\right]\ .

There are also canonical derived enhancements of these stacks: letting

Z^{h}_{\textbf{d}}(Q,W):=\textup{dCrit}(\textup{Tr}(W)_{\textbf{d}})=\Gamma_{d\textup{Tr}(W)_{\textbf{d}}}\times^{h}_{T^{\vee}X_{\textbf{d}}}X_{\textbf{d}}\ .

the derived stack of representations of the quiver with potential
(Q,W)
is defined by

\mathfrak{M}^{h}_{\textbf{d}}(Q,W)=\bigsqcup_{{\textbf{d}}\in\mathbb{N}^{V_{Q}}}\mathfrak{M}^{h}_{\textbf{d}}(Q,W)\quad\quad\textup{where}\quad\quad\mathfrak{M}^{h}_{\textbf{d}}(Q,W)=\left[Z^{h}_{\textbf{d}}(Q,W)/G_{\textbf{d}}(Q)\right]\ .

There are subspaces
X_{\textbf{d}}^{\textup{nil}}(Q)\subset X_{\textbf{d}}(Q)
defined by

X_{\textbf{d}}^{\textup{nil}}(Q)=\{\varphi\in\Hom_{\textup{Alg}_{\textup{Ass}}(S{\textup{-BiMod}})}({\mathbb{K}}Q,{\underline{\textup{End}}}({\mathbb{K}}^{\textbf{d}}))\ |\ \varphi({\mathbb{K}}Q_{(n)})=\{0\}\ \subset{\underline{\textup{End}}}({\mathbb{K}}^{\textbf{d}})\ \textup{for $n\gg 0$}\}\ ,

and in turn a substack
\mathfrak{M}^{\textup{nil}}(Q)\subset\mathfrak{M}(Q)
defined by

\mathfrak{M}^{\textup{nil}}(Q)=\bigsqcup_{{\textbf{d}}\in\mathbb{N}^{V_{Q}}}\mathfrak{M}^{\textup{nil}}_{\textbf{d}}(Q)\quad\quad\textup{where}\quad\quad\mathfrak{M}_{\textbf{d}}^{\textup{nil}}(Q)=\left[X_{\textbf{d}}^{\textup{nil}}(Q)/G_{\textbf{d}}(Q)\right]\ .

Similarly, there are also subvarieties
Z_{\textbf{d}}^{\textup{nil}}(Q,R)\subset Z_{\textbf{d}}(Q,R)
and
Z_{\textbf{d}}^{\textup{nil}}(Q,W)\subset Z_{\textbf{d}}(Q,W)
defined by

Z_{\textbf{d}}^{\textup{nil}}(Q,R)=Z_{\textbf{d}}(Q,R)\times_{X_{\textbf{d}}(Q)}X_{\textbf{d}}^{\textup{nil}}(Q)\quad\quad\text{and}\quad\quad Z_{\textbf{d}}^{\textup{nil}}(Q,W)=Z_{\textbf{d}}(Q,W)\times_{X_{\textbf{d}}(Q)}X_{\textbf{d}}^{\textup{nil}}(Q)\ ,

and in turn closed substacks
\mathfrak{M}^{\textup{nil}}(Q,R)
and
\mathfrak{M}^{\textup{nil}}(Q,W)\subset\mathfrak{M}^{\textup{nil}}(Q)
defined by

\mathfrak{M}^{\textup{nil}}(Q,R)=\bigsqcup_{{\textbf{d}}\in\mathbb{N}^{V_{Q}}}\mathfrak{M}^{\textup{nil}}_{\textbf{d}}(Q,R)\quad\quad\textup{where}\quad\quad\mathfrak{M}_{\textbf{d}}^{\textup{nil}}(Q,R)=\left[Z_{\textbf{d}}^{\textup{nil}}(Q,R)/G_{\textbf{d}}(Q)\right]\ ,

and similarly

\mathfrak{M}^{\textup{nil}}(Q,W)=\bigsqcup_{{\textbf{d}}\in\mathbb{N}^{V_{Q}}}\mathfrak{M}^{\textup{nil}}_{\textbf{d}}(Q,W)\quad\quad\textup{where}\quad\quad\mathfrak{M}_{\textbf{d}}^{\textup{nil}}(Q,W)=\left[Z_{\textbf{d}}^{\textup{nil}}(Q,W)/G_{\textbf{d}}(Q)\right]\ .

We now recall a general construction of the moduli of objects in an abelian category, following for example Definition 7.8 of
[
AHLH18
]
. Throughout, we let
\mathcal{C}
be a locally Noetherian, cocomplete,
\mathbb{K}
-linear abelian category.

Definition 3.30
.

Let
R
be a commutative
\mathbb{K}
algebra. The base change category
\mathcal{C}_{R}
of
\mathcal{C}
is defined to be the category of
R
-module objects internal to
\mathcal{C}
, that is, pairs
(C,\xi_{C})
of an object
C\in\mathcal{C}
together with a map of
\mathbb{K}
algebras
\xi_{R}:R\to{\textup{End}}_{\mathcal{C}}(C)
.

Definition 3.31
.

The moduli stack
\mathfrak{M}_{\mathcal{C}}
of objects of
\mathcal{C}
is defined by

\mathfrak{M}_{\mathcal{C}}(R)=\{E\in\mathcal{C}_{R}\ \big|\ \textup{$E$ is flat over $R$ and compact}\ \}\ ,

for each commutative
\mathbb{K}
algebra
R
.

It is shown in
loc. cit.
that
\mathfrak{M}_{\mathcal{C}}
indeed defines a stack in the big fppf topology on
\mathbb{K}
schemes. More generally, if
\mathcal{C}
is a non-cocomplete, locally Noetherian,
\mathbb{K}
-linear abelian category, we write
\mathfrak{M}_{\mathcal{C}}:=\mathfrak{M}_{\textup{Ind}(\mathcal{C})}
, and we recall that the finitely presented (or equivalently, compact) objects of
\textup{Ind}(\mathcal{C})
are given by the objects of
\mathcal{C}
, noting that
\mathcal{C}
is abelian and thus idempotent-complete.

We can now state the main result of this subsection. For simplicity, we introduce the notation

\mathfrak{M}(Y):=\mathfrak{M}_{\textup{PervCoh}_{\textup{cs}}(\hat{Y})}\ .

Then we have:

Theorem 3.32
.

Let
Y\xrightarrow{\pi}X
be a toric resolution of singularities of an affine, toric, Calabi-Yau threefold, such that the fibres of
\pi
are of dimension
\leq 1
and
\pi_{*}\mathcal{O}_{Y}\cong\mathcal{O}_{X}
, and let
(Q_{Y},W_{Y})
be the associated quiver with potential. There is an equivalence of algebraic stacks

(3.37)

\mathfrak{M}^{\textup{nil}}(Q_{Y},W_{Y})\xrightarrow{\cong}\mathfrak{M}(Y)

where the induced equivalence of groupoids of
\mathbb{K}
points is defined on objects by

\hskip-28.45274pt(V_{i},B_{ij})\mapsto\left(\tilde{H}:=\bigoplus_{i\in I}K(I_{i})\otimes V_{i}\ ,\ d_{B}:=\sum_{k\in\mathbb{Z},\ i,i_{2},...,i_{k-1},j\in I}K(m_{k}^{\Sigma}(\cdot,b_{i,i_{2}},...,b_{i_{k-1},j})^{N})\otimes(B_{i,i_{2}}...B_{i_{k-2},j})\right)\ ,

in the notation of Section
3.4
.

Similarly, this induces an equivalence of the homotopy
T
fixed points

\mathfrak{M}(Q_{Y},W_{Y})^{T}\xrightarrow{\cong}\mathfrak{M}_{\textup{PervCoh}_{\textup{cs}}(Y)^{T}}\ .

The main remaining ingredient of the proof is the following standard fact:

Lemma 3.33
.

Let
\Lambda=\mathbb{K}\langle Q\rangle_{R}
be the path algebra of a quiver with relations
(Q,R)
and
\hat{\Lambda}
its completion with respect to the filtration by path length. There are equivalences of algebraic stacks

\mathfrak{M}(Q,R)\xrightarrow{\cong}\mathfrak{M}_{\Lambda{\textup{-Mod}}_{\textup{Fd}}}\quad\quad\text{and}\quad\quad\mathfrak{M}^{\textup{nil}}(Q,R)\xrightarrow{\cong}\mathfrak{M}_{\hat{\Lambda}{\textup{-Mod}}_{\textup{Fd}}}\ .

Proof.

This is a standard result, but we give a proof a generalization of it in Lemma
3.33
; taking
{\textbf{d}}=({\textbf{d}}_{0},0)\in\mathbb{N}^{V_{Q}}\times\{0\}\subset\mathbb{N}^{V_{Q_{M}}}
in
loc. cit.
gives precisely this proposition, by commutativity of the diagram in Equation
4.17
.
∎

Proof.

(of Theorem
3.32

The definition of the moduli of objects functor is evidently natural with respect to equivalences of categories, so that we obtain a canonical equivalence of algebraic stacks

\mathfrak{M}_{\hat{\Lambda}{\textup{-Mod}}_{\textup{Fr}}}\xrightarrow{\cong}\mathfrak{M}_{\textup{PervCoh}_{\textup{cs}}(\hat{Y})},

by the equivalence of Theorem
3.20
. Composing with the equivalence of algebraic stacks of Proposition
3.33
yields the desired equivalence of Equation
3.37
, and the induced equivalence on groupoids of
\mathbb{K}
points is defined on objects by the claimed formula, by Proposition
3.29
. Finally, we note that the quiver with relations determined by
\Sigma
is in fact a quiver with potential, by Example
2.35
above.
∎

so that the monad formalism of Proposition
3.26
, which determines the resolution
(\tilde{H},d)
of an object
H\in\textup{Coh}_{\textup{cs}}(\mathbb{C}^{3})
in terms of the corresponding quiver representation
V
, is given by

(3.40)

\mathcal{O}\otimes V\xrightarrow{\scriptsize{\begin{pmatrix}B_{1}-x\\
y-B_{2}\\
B_{3}-z\end{pmatrix}}}\mathcal{O}^{3}\otimes V\xrightarrow{\scriptsize{\begin{pmatrix}0&B_{3}-z&B_{2}-y\\
B_{3}-z&0&x-B_{1}\\
y-B_{2}&x-B_{1}&0\end{pmatrix}}}\mathcal{O}^{3}\otimes V\xrightarrow{\scriptsize{\begin{pmatrix}x-B_{1}&y-B_{2}&z-B_{3}\end{pmatrix}}}\mathcal{O}\otimes V\ ,

with
\dim V=n
given by the coefficient of the
K
theory class of
H
in terms of the simple object
[H]=n[F]
, or equivalently the length of the corresponding pure sheaf of dimension
0
.

Example 3.35
.

Let
Y=|\mathcal{O}_{\mathbb{P}^{1}}\oplus\mathcal{O}_{\mathbb{P}^{1}}(-2)|\to X=Y^{\textup{aff}}\cong{\textup{Spec}\ }{\mathbb{C}}[x_{1},x_{2},x_{3},x_{4}]/(x_{1}x_{2}-x_{3}^{2})
so that the simple objects in
\textup{PervCoh}_{\textup{cs}}(Y)
are given by
F_{0}=\iota_{*}\mathcal{O}_{\mathbb{P}^{1}}
and
F_{1}=\iota_{*}\mathcal{O}_{\mathbb{P}^{1}}(-1)[1]
.

The algebra
\Sigma
can be computed explicitly as follows: let
\tilde{F}_{0}=\mathcal{O}_{\mathbb{P}^{1}}
and
\tilde{F}_{1}=\mathcal{O}_{\mathbb{P}^{1}}(-1)[1]
, and for simplicity we drop the dependence on
\mathbb{P}^{1}
from the notation. Then we have

\Sigma=\bigoplus_{i,j=0,1}\ {}_{j}\Sigma_{i}\cong\bigoplus_{i,j=0,1}\Ext^{\bullet}(F_{i},F_{j}\otimes\textup{Sym}^{\bullet}((\mathcal{O}\oplus\mathcal{O}(-2))[-1]))\ ,

so that we have

{}_{0}\Sigma_{0}

\displaystyle:=\Ext^{\bullet}(\mathcal{O}(-1)[1],\mathcal{O}(-1)[1]\otimes\textup{Sym}^{\bullet}((\mathcal{O}\oplus\mathcal{O}(-2))[-1]))

\displaystyle=\Ext^{0}(\mathcal{O},\mathcal{O})\oplus\Ext^{0}(\mathcal{O},\mathcal{O})[-1]\oplus\Ext^{1}(\mathcal{O},\mathcal{O}(-2))[-2]\oplus\Ext^{1}(\mathcal{O},\mathcal{O}(-2))[-3]

\displaystyle\cong{\mathbb{K}}\oplus{\mathbb{K}}[-1]\oplus{\mathbb{K}}[-2]\oplus{\mathbb{K}}[-3]

{}_{1}\Sigma_{1}

\displaystyle:=\Ext^{\bullet}(\mathcal{O},\textup{Sym}^{\bullet}((\mathcal{O}\oplus\mathcal{O}(-2))[-1]))

\displaystyle=\Ext^{0}(\mathcal{O},\mathcal{O})\oplus\Ext^{0}(\mathcal{O},\mathcal{O})[-1]\oplus\Ext^{1}(\mathcal{O},\mathcal{O}(-2))[-2]\oplus\Ext^{1}(\mathcal{O},\mathcal{O}(-2))[-3]

\displaystyle\cong{\mathbb{K}}\oplus{\mathbb{K}}[-1]\oplus{\mathbb{K}}[-2]\oplus{\mathbb{K}}[-3]

{}_{1}\Sigma_{0}

\displaystyle:=\Ext^{\bullet}(\mathcal{O}(-1)[1],\textup{Sym}^{\bullet}((\mathcal{O}\oplus\mathcal{O}(-2))[-1]))

\displaystyle\cong\Ext^{0}(\mathcal{O},\mathcal{O}(1))[-1]\oplus\Ext^{0}(\mathcal{O},\mathcal{O}(1))[-2]

\displaystyle\cong{\mathbb{K}}^{2}[-1]\oplus{\mathbb{K}}^{2}[-2]

{}_{0}\Sigma_{1}

\displaystyle:=\Ext^{\bullet}(\mathcal{O},\mathcal{O}(-1)[1]\otimes\textup{Sym}^{\bullet}((\mathcal{O}\oplus\mathcal{O}(-2))[-1]))

\displaystyle\cong\Ext^{1}(\mathcal{O},\mathcal{O}(-3))[-1]\oplus\Ext^{1}(\mathcal{O},\mathcal{O}(-3))[-2]

\displaystyle\cong{\mathbb{K}}^{2}[-1]\oplus{\mathbb{K}}^{2}[-2]

.

and the corresponding quiver with potential
(Q_{Y},W_{Y})
is given by

{}{}{}}}{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}\hss}\lxSVG@discardpath\lxSVG@closescope \hss}}\lxSVG@closescope\endpgfpicture}}\quad\quad\text{and}\quad\quad W_{Y}=E(BC-DA)+F(AD-CB)\ .

The compactly supported objects
F_{0}=\iota_{*}\mathcal{O}_{\mathbb{P}^{1}}
and
F_{1}=\iota_{*}\mathcal{O}_{\mathbb{P}^{1}}(-1)[1]
corresponding to the two nodes of the quiver have projective resolutions determined by the injective
\Sigma
modules

\displaystyle I_{0}

\displaystyle=[S_{0}<S_{0}\oplus S_{1}^{\oplus 2}[1]<S_{0}\oplus S_{1}^{\oplus 2}[2]<S_{0}[3]]

\displaystyle I_{1}

\displaystyle=[S_{1}<S_{1}\oplus S_{0}^{\oplus 2}[1]<S_{1}\oplus S_{0}^{\oplus 2}[2]<S_{1}[3]]\ .

There is a single independent self extension class for each of the simple objects which both correspond to the map of coherent sheaves
y
, as well as two independent extension classes in each of the groups
\Ext^{1}_{\Sigma}(S_{1},S_{2})
and
\Ext^{1}_{\Sigma}(S_{2},S_{1})
, which correspond to the maps of coherent sheaves
1,z
and
x,y
, respectively, under the identifications

\displaystyle\Ext^{1}_{\Sigma}(S_{0},S_{0})

\displaystyle\cong(_{0}\Lambda_{0})^{1}\cong\Hom_{\mathbb{P}^{1}}(\mathcal{O}_{\mathbb{P}^{1}},\mathcal{O}_{\mathbb{P}^{1}})={\mathbb{C}}_{y}

\displaystyle\subset\ _{0}\Lambda_{0}=\Hom_{Y}(\mathcal{O},\mathcal{O})

\displaystyle\Ext^{1}_{\Sigma}(S_{1},S_{1})

\displaystyle\cong(_{1}\Lambda_{1})^{1}\cong\Hom_{\mathbb{P}^{1}}(\mathcal{O}_{\mathbb{P}^{1}},\mathcal{O}_{\mathbb{P}^{1}})={\mathbb{C}}_{y}

\displaystyle\subset\ _{1}\Lambda_{1}=\Hom_{Y}(\mathcal{O},\mathcal{O})

\displaystyle\Ext^{1}_{\Sigma}(S_{0},S_{1})

\displaystyle\cong(_{0}\Lambda_{1})^{1}\cong\Hom_{\mathbb{P}^{1}}(\mathcal{O}_{\mathbb{P}^{1}},\mathcal{O}_{\mathbb{P}^{1}}(1))={\mathbb{C}}^{2}_{1,z}

\displaystyle\subset\ _{0}\Lambda_{1}=\Hom_{Y}(\mathcal{O},\mathcal{O}(1))

\displaystyle\Ext^{1}_{\Sigma}(S_{1},S_{0})

\displaystyle\cong(_{1}\Lambda_{0})^{1}\cong\Hom_{\mathbb{P}^{1}}(\mathcal{O}_{\mathbb{P}^{1}},\mathcal{O}_{\mathbb{P}^{1}}(1))=\mathbb{C}_{x,xz}^{2}

\displaystyle\subset\ _{1}\Lambda_{0}=\Hom_{Y}(\mathcal{O}(1),\mathcal{O})

where
z
denotes some choice of local coordinate on the base
\mathbb{P}^{1}
and
x,y
denote the linear coordinates on the fibres of
\mathcal{O}(-2)
and
\mathcal{O}
, respectively. Thus, the resolutions of the simple objects
F_{i}
are given by

\displaystyle K(I_{0})

\displaystyle=[\mathcal{O}\xrightarrow{\scriptsize{\begin{pmatrix}y\\
1\\
z\end{pmatrix}}}\mathcal{O}\oplus\mathcal{O}(1)^{2}\xrightarrow{\scriptsize{\begin{pmatrix}0&xz&-x\\
-z&0&y\\
1&-y&0\end{pmatrix}}}\mathcal{O}\oplus\mathcal{O}(1)^{2}\xrightarrow{\scriptsize{\begin{pmatrix}y&x&xz\end{pmatrix}}}\mathcal{O}]\xrightarrow{\cong}s_{*}\mathcal{O}_{\mathbb{P}^{1}}=F_{0}

and

\displaystyle K(I_{1})

\displaystyle=[\mathcal{O}(1)\xrightarrow{\scriptsize{\begin{pmatrix}y\\
x\\
xz\end{pmatrix}}}\mathcal{O}(1)\oplus\mathcal{O}^{2}\xrightarrow{\scriptsize{\begin{pmatrix}0&z&-1\\
-xz&0&y\\
x&-y&0\end{pmatrix}}}\mathcal{O}(1)\oplus\mathcal{O}^{2}\xrightarrow{\scriptsize{\begin{pmatrix}y&1&z\end{pmatrix}}}\mathcal{O}(1)]\xrightarrow{\cong}s_{*}\mathcal{O}_{\mathbb{P}^{1}}(-1)[1]=F_{1}

\displaystyle\ .

The maps between these resolutions corresponding to the generators of
\Sigma^{1}
are given by:

Example 3.36
.

Let
Y=|\mathcal{O}_{\mathbb{P}^{1}}(-1)\oplus\mathcal{O}_{\mathbb{P}^{1}}(-1)|\to X=Y^{\textup{aff}}\cong{\textup{Spec}\ }{\mathbb{C}}[x_{1},x_{2},x_{3},x_{4}]/(x_{1}x_{2}-x_{3}x_{4})
so that the simple objects in
\textup{PervCoh}_{\textup{cs}}(Y)
are given by
F_{0}=\iota_{*}\mathcal{O}_{\mathbb{P}^{1}}
and
F_{1}=\iota_{*}\mathcal{O}_{\mathbb{P}^{1}}(-1)[1]
, as in the previous example.

The algebra
\Sigma
can be computed explicitly, as in the previous example, by

\Sigma=\bigoplus_{i,j=0,1}\ {}_{i}\Sigma_{j}\cong\bigoplus_{i,j=0,1}\Ext^{\bullet}(F_{i},F_{j}\otimes\textup{Sym}^{\bullet}((\mathcal{O}(-1)\oplus\mathcal{O}(-1))[-1]))

where we have

{}_{0}\Sigma_{0}

\displaystyle:=\Ext^{\bullet}(\mathcal{O}(-1)[1],\mathcal{O}(-1)[1]\otimes\textup{Sym}^{\bullet}((\mathcal{O}(-1)\oplus\mathcal{O}(-1))[-1]))

\displaystyle\cong\Ext^{0}(\mathcal{O},\mathcal{O})\oplus\Ext^{1}(\mathcal{O},\mathcal{O}(-2))[-3]

\displaystyle\cong{\mathbb{K}}\oplus{\mathbb{K}}[-3]

{}_{1}\Sigma_{1}

\displaystyle:=\Ext^{\bullet}(\mathcal{O},\textup{Sym}^{\bullet}((\mathcal{O}(-1)\oplus\mathcal{O}(-1))[-1]))

\displaystyle\cong\Ext^{0}(\mathcal{O},\mathcal{O})\oplus\Ext^{1}(\mathcal{O},\mathcal{O}(-2))[-3]

\displaystyle\cong{\mathbb{K}}\oplus{\mathbb{K}}[-3]

{}_{0}\Sigma_{1}

\displaystyle:=\Ext^{\bullet}(\mathcal{O},\mathcal{O}(-1)[1]\otimes\textup{Sym}^{\bullet}((\mathcal{O}(-1)\oplus\mathcal{O}(-1))[-1]))

\displaystyle\cong\Ext^{1}(\mathcal{O},\mathcal{O}(-2))^{\oplus 2}[-1]\oplus\Ext^{1}(\mathcal{O},\mathcal{O}(-3))[-2]

\displaystyle\cong{\mathbb{K}}^{2}[-1]\oplus{\mathbb{K}}^{2}[-2]

{}_{1}\Sigma_{0}

\displaystyle:=\Ext^{\bullet}(\mathcal{O}(-1)[1],\textup{Sym}^{\bullet}((\mathcal{O}(-1)\oplus\mathcal{O}(-1))[-1]))

\displaystyle\cong\Ext^{0}(\mathcal{O},\mathcal{O}(1))[-1]\Ext^{0}(\mathcal{O},\mathcal{O})^{\oplus 2}[-2]

\displaystyle\cong{\mathbb{K}}^{2}[-1]\oplus{\mathbb{K}}^{2}[-2]

Thus, the corresponding quiver with potential
(Q_{Y},W_{Y})
is given by

modules

\displaystyle I_{1}

\displaystyle=[S_{1}<S_{2}^{\oplus 2}[1]<S_{2}^{\oplus 2}[2]<S_{1}[3]]

\displaystyle I_{2}

\displaystyle=[S_{2}<S_{1}^{\oplus 2}[1]<S_{1}^{\oplus 2}[2]<S_{2}[3]]\ .

There are no non-trivial self extensions of the simple objects, while there are two independent extension classes in each of the groups
\Ext^{1}_{\Sigma}(S_{1},S_{2})
and
\Ext^{1}_{\Sigma}(S_{2},S_{1})
, which correspond to the maps of coherent sheaves
1,z
and
x,y
, respectively, under the identifications

\displaystyle\Ext^{1}_{\Sigma}(S_{1},S_{2})

\displaystyle\cong(_{1}\Lambda_{2})^{1}\cong\Hom_{\mathbb{P}^{1}}(\mathcal{O}_{\mathbb{P}^{1}},\mathcal{O}_{\mathbb{P}^{1}}(1))={\mathbb{C}}^{2}_{1,z}

\displaystyle\subset\ _{1}\Lambda_{2}=\Hom_{Y}(\mathcal{O},\mathcal{O}(1))

\displaystyle\Ext^{1}_{\Sigma}(S_{2},S_{1})

\displaystyle\cong(_{2}\Lambda_{1})^{1}\cong\Hom_{\mathbb{P}^{1}}(\mathcal{O}_{\mathbb{P}^{1}},\mathcal{O}_{\mathbb{P}^{1}}^{\oplus 2})=\mathbb{C}_{x,y}^{2}

\displaystyle\subset\ _{2}\Lambda_{1}=\Hom_{Y}(\mathcal{O}(1),\mathcal{O})

where
z
denotes some choice of local coordinate on the base
\mathbb{P}^{1}
and
x,y
denote the linear coordinates on the fibres of the rank two bundle. Thus, the resolutions of the simple objects
F_{i}
are given by

\displaystyle K(I_{1})

\displaystyle=[\mathcal{O}\xrightarrow{\scriptsize{\begin{pmatrix}1\\
z\end{pmatrix}}}\mathcal{O}(1)^{2}\xrightarrow{\scriptsize{\begin{pmatrix}zy&-y\\
-zx&x\end{pmatrix}}}\mathcal{O}(1)^{2}\xrightarrow{\scriptsize{\begin{pmatrix}x&y\end{pmatrix}}}\mathcal{O}]\xrightarrow{\cong}s_{*}\mathcal{O}_{\mathbb{P}^{1}}=F_{1}

\displaystyle K(I_{2})

\displaystyle=[\mathcal{O}(1)\xrightarrow{\scriptsize{\begin{pmatrix}x\\
y\end{pmatrix}}}\mathcal{O}^{2}\xrightarrow{\scriptsize{\begin{pmatrix}yz&-xz\\
-y&x\end{pmatrix}}}\mathcal{O}^{2}\xrightarrow{\scriptsize{\begin{pmatrix}1&z\end{pmatrix}}}\mathcal{O}(1)]\xrightarrow{\cong}s_{*}\mathcal{O}_{\mathbb{P}^{1}}(-1)[1]=F_{2}

The maps between these resolutions corresponding to the generators of
\Sigma^{1}
are given by:

3.8.
Koszul resolutions from Beilinson spectral sequences

In this section, we explain the existence of the canonical Koszul resolutions of perverse coherent sheaves described in Equation
3.21
, in terms of the Beilinson spectral sequence induced by a natural resolution of the diagonal in terms of the distinguished projective generators. Similar arguments feature in the proofs of some of the main results of
[
Bri02
]
,
[
Ber04b
]
,
[
Ber04a
]
, and
[
BKR01
]
, though in this section we follow most closely the explicit discussion in
[
Kin97
]
.

Warning 3.37
.

The results of this section will not be used in the remainder of the text, so the proofs are omitted for brevity. We recommend
[
Kin97
]
for statements of the results closest to the presentation here.

Throughout this section, let
Y
be a smooth variety,
E\in{\textup{D}}^{b}\textup{Coh}(Y)
a classical tilting object, and
\Lambda=\Hom_{{\textup{D}}^{b}\textup{Coh}(Y)}(E,E)
the (classical) associative algebra of endomorphisms of
E
. Then as above, we obtain inverse equivalences of triangulated categories

\Hom_{{\textup{D}}^{b}\textup{Coh}(Y)}(E,\cdot):{\textup{D}}^{b}\textup{Coh}(Y)\lx@xy@svg{\hbox{\raise 2.5pt\hbox{\kern 3.0pt\hbox{\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\hbox{\vtop{\halign{\entry@#!@&&\entry@@#!@\cr&\crcr}}}\ignorespaces{\hbox{\kern-3.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 3.0pt\raise-2.5pt\hbox{$\textstyle{\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}$}}}}}}}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces{}{\hbox{\lx@xy@droprule}}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces{\hbox{\kern 9.375pt\raise 8.30276pt\hbox{{}\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 3.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise-1.75pt\hbox{$\scriptstyle{\cong}$}}}\kern 3.0pt}}}}}}\ignorespaces{\hbox{\kern 27.0pt\raise 2.15277pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\lx@xy@tip{1}\lx@xy@tip{-1}}}}}}{\hbox{\lx@xy@droprule}}{\hbox{\lx@xy@droprule}}{\hbox{\kern 27.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 3.0pt\raise-2.5pt\hbox{$\textstyle{\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}$}}}}}}}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces{}{\hbox{\lx@xy@droprule}}\ignorespaces{\hbox{\kern 3.0pt\raise-2.15277pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\lx@xy@tip{1}\lx@xy@tip{-1}}}}}}{\hbox{\lx@xy@droprule}}{\hbox{\lx@xy@droprule}}\ignorespaces}}}}\ignorespaces{\textup{D}_{\textup{perf}}}(\Lambda):(\cdot)\otimes_{\Lambda}E\ ,

so that in particular we obtain a natural isomorphism

(3.81)

\Hom_{{\textup{D}}^{b}\textup{Coh}(Y)}(E,H)\otimes_{\Lambda}E\xrightarrow{\cong}H

for each object
H\in{\textup{D}}^{b}\textup{Coh}(Y)
.

The notions of
\Lambda
modules in
{\textup{D}}^{b}\textup{Coh}(Y)
and their tensor products with objects in
{\textup{D}}(\Lambda)
occuring in the preceding expressions are defined because
{\textup{D}}^{b}\textup{Coh}(Y)
is tensored over
\DGV
. In general, the tensor product of two objects
H_{1}\in\Lambda{\textup{-Mod}}({\textup{D}}^{b}\textup{Coh}(Y)),H_{2}\in\Lambda{\textup{-Mod}}({\textup{D}}^{b}\textup{Coh}(Y))
can be defined in terms of the induced algebra
\Lambda_{\mathcal{O}_{Y}}=\Lambda\otimes_{\mathbb{K}}\mathcal{O}_{Y}\in\textup{Alg}_{\textup{Ass}}({\textup{D}}^{b}\textup{Coh}(Y))
by

H_{1}\otimes_{\Lambda}H_{2}=H_{1}\otimes_{\Lambda_{\mathcal{O}_{Y}}}H_{2}

where on the right hand side the objects
H_{i}
are interpreted in the usual sense of module objects over an algebra object internal to the same category
{\textup{D}}^{b}\textup{Coh}(Y)
. Similarly, one defines

H_{1}\boxtimes_{\Lambda}H_{2}=\pi_{1}^{*}H_{1}\otimes_{\Lambda_{\mathcal{O}_{Y\times Y}}}\pi_{2}^{*}H_{2}\quad\in{\textup{D}}^{b}\textup{Coh}(Y\times Y)\ ,

which satisfies the usual identification

\Delta^{*}(H_{1}\boxtimes_{\Lambda}H_{2})=H_{1}\otimes_{\Lambda}H_{2}\ .

Now, taking
H=\mathcal{O}_{Y}
, the isomorphism of Equation
3.81
is given by

E^{\vee}\otimes_{\Lambda}E\xrightarrow{\cong}\mathcal{O}_{Y}\quad\quad\text{inducing a map}\quad\quad E^{\vee}\boxtimes_{\Lambda}E\to\Delta_{*}\mathcal{O}_{Y}

under the
(\Delta^{*},\Delta_{*})
adjunction. Moreover, we have:

Proposition 3.38
.

[
Kin97
]
Let
E\in\textup{Coh}(Y)
a classical tilting object which is in addition a vector bundle. Then the natural map

E^{\vee}\boxtimes_{\Lambda}E\xrightarrow{\cong}\Delta_{*}\mathcal{O}_{Y}

is an isomorphism.

Concretely, the resulting resolution of the diagonal can be computed explicitly as follows: given a projective resolution of
\Lambda
as a
(\Lambda,\Lambda)
bimodule

Q^{\bullet}=\left[\cdots\to Q^{i}\to\cdots\to Q^{-1}\to Q^{0}\right]\xrightarrow{\cong}\Lambda\ ,

the exterior tensor product is computed by the complex

(3.82)

E^{\vee}\boxtimes^{\bullet}_{\Lambda}E:=\left[\pi_{1}^{*}E^{\vee}\otimes_{\Lambda_{\mathcal{O}_{Y\times Y}}}Q^{\bullet}_{\mathcal{O}_{Y\times Y}}\otimes_{\Lambda_{\mathcal{O}_{Y\times Y}}}\pi_{2}^{*}E\right]\xrightarrow{\cong}E^{\vee}\boxtimes_{\Lambda}E\ .

Now, we return to the setting of the preceding section, and suppose
Y
is a quiver-accessible variety with distinguished projective objects
E_{i}
and simple objects
F_{i}
in
{\textup{D}}^{b}\textup{Coh}(Y)
with corresponding
\Lambda
modules
P_{i}
and
S_{i}
, so that
\Lambda
is equivalent to the path algebra of a DG quiver determined by
\Sigma=\Ext_{{\textup{D}}(\Lambda)}^{\bullet}(S,S)
. In particular, we also assume that the objects
E_{i}
are vector bundles.

In this setting, there is a natural projective resolution of
\Lambda
as a
(\Lambda,\Lambda)
bimodule with

Q^{k}=\bigoplus_{i,j\in V_{Q}}\Lambda S_{i}\otimes_{\mathbb{K}}(S_{i}\Sigma^{k}S_{j})^{\vee}\otimes_{\mathbb{K}}S_{j}\Lambda\ ,

where
i,j
runs over
V_{Q}
the index set of the distinguished projective objects, which is by definition the vertex set of the corresponding quiver
Q
; the resolution is determined by the identifications

\Lambda=\Lambda\otimes_{S}S\otimes_{\Lambda}S\otimes_{S}\Lambda\cong\Lambda\otimes_{S}((\otimes^{\bullet}_{S}\bar{\Lambda}[1])\otimes_{S}\Lambda)\otimes_{\Lambda}S\otimes_{S}\Lambda\cong\Lambda\otimes_{S}\Sigma^{\vee}\otimes_{S}\Lambda

where we have used the Koszul resolution of
\Lambda
together with the identification
(\otimes^{\bullet}_{S}\bar{\Lambda}[1])\cong\Sigma^{\vee}
. The resulting resolution of the diagonal in Equation
3.82
above is thus

E^{\vee}\boxtimes^{\bullet}_{\Lambda}E=\left[\bigoplus_{i,j\in V_{Q}}\pi_{1}^{*}E_{i}^{\vee}\otimes(S_{i}\Sigma^{\bullet}S_{j})_{\mathcal{O}_{Y^{\times 2}}}^{\vee}\otimes\pi_{2}^{*}E_{j}\right]\xrightarrow{\cong}\Delta_{*}\mathcal{O}_{Y}\ .

Now, given an arbitrary object
H\in\textup{PervCoh}_{\textup{cs}}(Y)^{{\mathbb{C}}^{\times}}
, we obtain a canonical resolution of
H
via the Beilinson spectral sequence associated to the above resolution of the diagonal: following the standard argument, we have a canonical isomorphism

H\cong\pi_{2*}\left(\pi_{1}^{*}H\otimes\Delta_{*}\mathcal{O}_{Y}\right).

and the Grothendieck spectral sequence for the composition of derived functors, computed using the resolution of the diagonal constructed above, yields the canonical resolution

(3.83)

\left[\bigoplus_{i,j\in V_{Q}}\Hom_{{\textup{D}}^{b}\textup{Coh}(Y)}(E_{i},H)\otimes_{\mathbb{K}}(S_{i}\Sigma^{\bullet}S_{j})^{\vee}\otimes_{\mathbb{K}}E_{j}\right]\xrightarrow{\cong}H\ ,

so that by construction, we have:

Proposition 3.39
.

Under the equivalence
\Lambda{\textup{-Mod}}\xrightarrow{\cong}\textup{PervCoh}(Y)^{{\mathbb{C}}^{\times}}
, the resolutions of objects in
\Lambda{\textup{-Mod}}
constructed in terms of Koszul duality, as in Equation
3.21
, are canonically identified with those induced by the Beilinson spectral sequence, as in Equation
3.83
.

4.
Perverse coherent extensions on Calabi-Yau threefolds and extended quivers

4.1.
Overview of Section
4

Let
\pi:X\to Y
be as in Section
3.2
. In this section, we extend the results of Theorems
3.11
,
3.27
, and
3.32
to describe certain categories generated by iterated extensions of compactly supported perverse coherent sheaves on
Y
together with an auxiliary object
M\in{\textup{D}}^{b}\textup{Coh}(Y)^{T}
which does not necessarily have compact support. These descriptions are given in terms of finite rank representations of an
extended
quiver, in a sense we will explain below. We recommend the reader consult the description of the motivation for these constructions given in Section
1.1
of the introduction prior to reading this section.

Throughout this section, we suppose that
M\in{\textup{D}}^{b}\textup{Coh}(Y)^{T}
satisfies the following hypotheses:

(1)

The algebra
\Ext^{0}(M,M)
is commutative,

(2)

\Ext^{i}(F,M)=0
and
\Ext^{i}(M,F)=0
for all
i\leq 0
and
F\in\textup{PervCoh}_{\textup{cs}}(Y)
, and

(3)

M\in\textup{PervCoh}^{\textup{p}}(Y)
lies in the heart of an admissible Bridgeland-Deligne perverse coherent t-structure on
Y
, in the sense of Definitions
4.10
and
4.11
, and in particular
\Ext^{i}(M,M)=0
for all
i<0
.

In Section
4.2
, we introduce the Bridgeland-Deligne perverse coherent t-structures used in the above hypotheses. In Sections
4.3
,
4.4
, and
4.5
we explain the analogues of the results of Sections
3.3
,
3.4
and
2.4
in the setting of perverse coherent extensions. In Section
4.6
, we define the notion of framing structures and prove Theorem
A
from the introduction. In Section
4.7
, we explain many examples of these constructions relevant to the applications to representation theory in Section
6
.

4.2.
Bridgeland-Deligne t-structures

To begin, we recall the classical theory of tilting
t
-structures by torsion theories.

Definition 4.1
.

Let
\mathcal{B}
be an abelian category. A torsion theory on
\mathcal{B}
is a pair
(\mathcal{T},\mathcal{F})
of full subcategories of
\mathcal{B}
such that

(1)

\Hom(T,F)=0
for each
T\in\mathcal{T}
and
F\in\mathcal{F}
, and

(2)

for each
E\in\mathcal{B}
there is a short exact sequence

0\to T\to E\to F\to 0

with
T\in\mathcal{T}
and
F\in\mathcal{F}
.

Let
\mathcal{D}
be a triangulated category with
t
-structure
({\mathcal{D}}^{\leq 0},{\mathcal{D}}^{\geq 0})
and heart
\mathcal{B}={\mathcal{D}}^{\leq 0}\cap{\mathcal{D}}^{\geq 0}
. Then, given a torsion theory
(\mathcal{T},\mathcal{F})
on
\mathcal{B}
, define

{\mathcal{D}}_{t}^{\leq 0}=\{E\in{\mathcal{D}}^{\leq 0}\ |\ H^{0}E\in\mathcal{T}\}\quad\quad\text{and}\quad\quad{\mathcal{D}}_{t}^{\geq 0}=\{E\in{\mathcal{D}}^{\geq-1}\ |\ H^{-1}E\in\mathcal{F}\}\ .

Proposition 4.2
.

The pair
({\mathcal{D}}_{t}^{\leq 0},{\mathcal{D}}_{t}^{\geq 0})
defines a
t
-structure on
{\mathcal{D}}
.

Proof.

See for example Proposition 2.1 of
[
HRS96
]
.
∎

The heart of this
t
-structure is given by

\mathcal{B}_{t}:=\{E\in{\mathcal{D}}^{[-1,0]}\ |\ H^{0}E\in\mathcal{T},\ H^{-1}E\in\mathcal{F}\}\ ,

or more concretely, if
{\mathcal{D}}
is the derived category of the abelian category
\mathcal{B}
with the standard
t
structure, then
\mathcal{B}_{t}
is the full subcategory of two-term complexes of the form

\mathcal{B}_{t}=\{E=\left[E^{-1}[1]\xrightarrow{\varphi}E^{0}\right]\ \bigg|\ E^{i}\in\mathcal{B},\ \textup{coker}\varphi\in\mathcal{T},\ \ker\varphi\in\mathcal{F}\}\ .

In particular, we have:

Corollary 4.3
.

\mathcal{B}_{t}
is an abelian category.

Example 4.4
.

Let
\mathcal{B}=\textup{Coh}(X)
be the abelian category of coherent sheaves on
X
an irreducible algebraic variety of dimension
d
,
\mathcal{T}
the full subcategory on objects with support of dimension
\leq d-1
, and
\mathcal{F}
the full subcategory on torsion free coherent sheaves on
X
. There are evidently no possible maps
\mathcal{T}
to
\mathcal{F}
, and for each
E\in\textup{Coh}(X)
, the torsion filtration

0\to T_{d-1}E\to E\to E/T_{d-1}E\to 0

gives the required short exact sequence, where
T_{d-1}E
denotes the maximal subsheaf of
E
with support of dimension
\leq d-1
.

The resulting tilted category
\mathcal{B}_{t}
is given by

\mathcal{B}_{t}=\{E=\left[E^{-1}[1]\xrightarrow{\varphi}E^{0}\right]\ \bigg|\ E^{i}\in\textup{Coh}(X),\ \dim\textup{supp}H^{0}E\leq d-1,\ H^{-1}E\textup{ is torsion free}\ \}\ .

More generally, we have:

Example 4.5
.

Let
\mathcal{B}=\textup{Coh}(X)
as in the previous example,
\mathcal{T}=\textup{Coh}_{\leq k}(X)
the full subcategory on objects with support of dimension
\leq k
, and

\mathcal{F}=\textup{Coh}_{\geq k+1}(X):=\mathcal{T}^{\perp}\ ,

the right orthogonal to
\mathcal{T}
. Since
\mathcal{B}
is Noetherian and
\mathcal{T}
is closed under extensions and quotients, we have that
(\mathcal{T},\mathcal{F})
is a torsion pair. The resulting tilted category
\mathcal{B}_{t}
is given by

\mathcal{B}_{t}=\{E=\left[E^{-1}[1]\xrightarrow{\varphi}E^{0}\right]\ \bigg|\ E^{i}\in\textup{Coh}(X),\ \dim\textup{supp}\ H^{0}E\leq k,\ H^{-1}E\in\textup{Coh}_{\geq k+1}(X)\ \}\ .

Another variant of this construction is to use coherent sheaves supported along a particular subvariety:

Example 4.6
.

Let
\mathcal{B}=\textup{Coh}(X)
as in the previous example, and fix a closed subvariety
Z\subset X
. Then let
\mathcal{T}=\textup{Coh}_{Z}(X)
denote the full subcategory on objects supported on
Z
and
\mathcal{F}=\mathcal{T}^{\perp}
. Since
\mathcal{B}
is Noetherian and
\mathcal{T}
is closed under extensions and quotients, we have that
(\mathcal{T},\mathcal{F})
is a torsion pair. The resulting tilted category
\mathcal{B}_{t}
is given by

\mathcal{B}_{t}=\{E=\left[E^{-1}[1]\xrightarrow{\varphi}E^{0}\right]\ \bigg|\ E^{i}\in\textup{Coh}(X),\ \textup{supp}\ H^{0}E\subset Z,\ H^{-1}E\in\textup{Coh}_{Z}(X)^{\perp}\ \}\ .

In fact, the previous construction can be iterated to define a family of t-structures on the derived category of coherent sheaves; this construction is recorded in
[
AB10
]
, following unpublished results of Deligne. Similar results appeared in
[
Gab04
]
and
[
Kas04
]
, and we recommend the latter for a more explicit explanation of the geometric interpretation of the perversity function. We now recall the general definition:

Definition 4.7
.

Let
X
be a variety and
X^{\textup{top}}
denote the Zariski topological space underlying
X
. A (monotone and comonotone)
perversity function

{\textup{p}}:X^{\textup{top}}\to\mathbb{Z}
is a function such that

{\textup{p}}(y)\geq{\textup{p}}(x)\quad\quad\text{and}\quad\quad{\textup{p}}(y)\leq{\textup{p}}(x)+\dim(x)-\dim(y)\quad\quad\text{for any}\quad y\in\overline{\{x\}}\ .

Given a perversity function
{\textup{p}}:X^{\textup{top}}\to\mathbb{Z}
, the
Deligne perverse coherent t-structure
associated to
p
is defined by

\displaystyle{\textup{D}}^{b}\textup{Coh}(X)^{{\textup{p}},\leq 0}

\displaystyle:=\{E\in{\textup{D}}^{b}\textup{Coh}(Y)\ |\ \iota_{x}^{*}E\in{\textup{D}}^{\leq{\textup{p}}(x)}(\mathcal{O}_{x})\ \textup{for any $x\in X^{\textup{top}}$}\}

,

\displaystyle{\textup{D}}^{b}\textup{Coh}(X)^{{\textup{p}},\geq 0}

\displaystyle:=\{E\in{\textup{D}}^{b}\textup{Coh}(Y)\ |\ \iota_{x}^{!}E\in{\textup{D}}^{\geq{\textup{p}}(x)}(\mathcal{O}_{x})\ \textup{for any $x\in X^{\textup{top}}$}\}

.

Indeed, we have the following result:

Theorem 4.8
.

[
AB10
]
The pair
({\textup{D}}^{b}\textup{Coh}(X)^{{\textup{p}},\leq 0},{\textup{D}}^{b}\textup{Coh}(X)^{{\textup{p}},\geq 0})
defines a t-structure on
{\textup{D}}^{b}\textup{Coh}(X)
.

Proof.

See Theorem in
[
AB10
]
.
∎

We introduce the notation
\textup{PervCoh}^{\textup{p}}(X)
to denote the category of Deligne perverse coherent sheaves on
X
associated to perversity function
p

These t-structures are often called simply perverse coherent t-structures. We use the prefix Deligne to avoid confusion with the notion of perverse coherent sheaf defined by Bridgeland, recalled in Definition
2.15
. In fact, the category of perverse coherent sheaves (in the sense of Bridgeland) can also be constructed by tilting the abelian category of coherent sheaves with respect to a torsion theory:

Example 4.9
.

Let
f:Y\to X
be as in Section
2.3
and let
\mathcal{C}^{\heartsuit}
denote the full subcategory of
\textup{Coh}(Y)
on objects
C
such that
f_{*}C=0
. Define full subcategories
\mathcal{T}
and
\mathcal{F}
of
\textup{Coh}(Y)
by

\displaystyle\mathcal{T}

\displaystyle=\{E\in\textup{Coh}(Y)\ |\ \mathbb{R}^{1}f_{*}T=0,\ \Hom(T,C)=0\ \text{for any $C\in\mathcal{C}^{\heartsuit}$}\ \}

\displaystyle\mathcal{F}

\displaystyle=\{E\in\textup{Coh}(Y)\ |\ \mathbb{R}^{0}f_{*}T=0\ \}\ .

From the first exact triangle of Equation
2.3
, one can check that the pair
(\mathcal{T},\mathcal{F})
defines a torsion theory on
\textup{Coh}(Y)
, and the resulting tilted category is equivalent to the category of perverse coherent sheaves,

\textup{Coh}(Y)_{t}=\textup{PervCoh}(Y)\ ,

by Corollary
2.18
.

We can now introduce the desired
t
-structures, which will be used to define the categories of perverse coherent extensions.

Definition 4.10
.

Let
f:Y\to X
be as in Section
2.3
, and let
{\textup{p}}:X^{\textup{top}}\to\mathbb{Z}
be a perversity function on
X
. The
Bridgeland-Deligne perverse coherent t-structure
associated to
p
is defined by

(4.1)

\displaystyle{\textup{D}}^{b}\textup{Coh}(Y)^{p,\leq 0}

\displaystyle:=\{E\in{\textup{D}}^{b}\textup{Coh}(Y)\ |\ f_{*}E\in{\textup{D}}^{b}\textup{Coh}(X)^{{\textup{p}},\leq 0}\text{ and }\iota^{L}E\in\mathcal{C}^{-1,\leq 0}\}

,

(4.2)

\displaystyle{\textup{D}}^{b}\textup{Coh}(Y)^{p,\geq 0}

\displaystyle:=\{E\in{\textup{D}}^{b}\textup{Coh}(Y)\ |\ f_{*}E\in{\textup{D}}^{b}\textup{Coh}(X)^{{\textup{p}},\geq 0}\text{ and }\iota^{R}E\in\mathcal{C}^{-1,\geq 0}\}

.

The category of Bridgeland-Deligne perverse coherent sheaves on
f:Y\to X
with respect to the perversity function
p
is the abelian category defined by

\textup{PervCoh}^{\textup{p}}(Y/X)={\textup{D}}^{b}\textup{Coh}(Y)^{{\textup{p}},\leq 0}\cap{\textup{D}}^{b}\textup{Coh}(Y)^{{\textup{p}},\geq 0}\ .

Note that this indeed defines a t-structure, by Proposition
2.14
and Theorem
2.11
, combined with Theorem
4.8
above. In particular, we make the following definition. As for the usual perverse coherent sheaves in the sense of Bridgeland, recalled in Definition
2.15
, we will often drop the dependence on
X
from the notation and write simply

\textup{PervCoh}^{\textup{p}}(Y):=\textup{PervCoh}^{\textup{p}}(Y/X)\ .

For our primary application of interest, it will be necessary to require the following additional hypothesis:

Definition 4.11
.

A Bridgeland-Deligne perverse coherent t-structure is called
admissible
if the corresponding heart satisfies

\textup{PervCoh}_{\textup{cs}}(Y)\subset\textup{PervCoh}^{\textup{p}}(Y)\ ,

that is, it contains the category of compactly supported perverse coherent sheaves.

Example 4.12
.

Let
X
be an affine variety and define the perversity function
{\textup{p}}:X^{\textup{top}}\to\mathbb{Z}
by
{\textup{p}}(x)=0
for each closed point
x\in X(\mathbb{K})
and
{\textup{p}}(y)=-1
otherwise. Then
\textup{PervCoh}^{\textup{p}}(X)=\textup{Coh}(X)_{t}
, the tilt of
\textup{Coh}(X)
with respect to the torsion theory
(\mathcal{T},\mathcal{F})
defined by
\mathcal{T}=\textup{Coh}_{\leq 0}(X)
and
\mathcal{F}=\mathcal{T}^{\perp}
, as in Example
4.5
.

Moreover, for
f:Y\to X
as in Section
2.3
, the Bridgeland-Deligne perverse coherent t-structure determined by
p
is admissible, and for any subvariety
Z\subset Y
of dimension
\geq 1
the object
M=\mathcal{O}_{Z}[1]\in\textup{PervCoh}^{\textup{p}}(Y)
.

Example 4.13
.

Let
X
be an affine variety and define the perversity function
{\textup{p}}:X^{\textup{top}}\to\mathbb{Z}
by
{\textup{p}}(x)=0
for each closed point
x\in X(\mathbb{K})
or one dimensional subvariety, and
{\textup{p}}(y)=-1
otherwise. Then
\textup{PervCoh}^{\textup{p}}(X)=\textup{Coh}(X)_{t}
, the tilt of
\textup{Coh}(X)
with respect to the torsion theory
(\mathcal{T},\mathcal{F})
defined by
\mathcal{T}=\textup{Coh}_{\leq 1}(X)
and
\mathcal{F}=\mathcal{T}^{\perp}
, as in Example
4.5
. We remark that a similar t-structure appeared in the proof of the main theorem of
[
Tod09
]
.

Moreover, for
f:Y\to X
as in Section
2.3
, the Bridgeland-Deligne perverse coherent t-structure determined by
p
is evidently admissible, and for any subvariety
Z\subset Y
of pure dimension
\geq 2
the object
M=\mathcal{O}_{Z}[1]\in\textup{PervCoh}^{\textup{p}}(Y)
, and similarly for any subvariety
Z
of pure dimension
\leq 1
the object
\mathcal{O}_{Z}\in\textup{PervCoh}^{\textup{p}}(Y)
.

4.3.
Categories of perverse coherent extensions

Let
\textup{Thick}(F\oplus M)
denote the thick subcategory of
{\textup{D}}^{b}\textup{Coh}(\hat{Y})
generated by the compactly supported simple objects
F_{i}
together with
M
, and similarly for the equivariant analogues. There are equivalent corresponding thick subcategories of
{\textup{D}}_{\textup{perf}}(\hat{\Lambda})
and
{\textup{D}}_{\textup{Fd}}(\Sigma)
, and their graded analogues, and we will describe them (as well as their hearts with respect to certain t-structures) in terms of explicit extensions of canonical resolutions determined by complexes of
\Sigma
, generalizing the descriptions given in Sections
3.2
,
3.3
and
3.4
of the images of the objects in
{\textup{D}}^{b}\textup{Coh}_{\textup{cs}}(Y)
(and in
\textup{PervCoh}_{\textup{cs}}(Y)
) under these equivalences.

In order to analogously parameterize this larger class of extensions, and ultimately give descriptions of the moduli stacks of objects of these categories, it will be necessary to first understand the category in terms of Morita theory for the object
F\oplus M
, which leads naturally to the extended quiver, as we now explain.

To begin, in analogy with Corollary
3.7
, letting

\Sigma_{M}=\Hom(F\oplus M,F\oplus M)\quad\quad\text{and}\quad\quad\Sigma_{\infty}=\Hom(M,M)\

denote the (graded) DG associative algebras of endomorphisms of
F\oplus M
and
M
, respectively, we have:

Corollary 4.14
.

There are equivalences of triangulated categories

\textup{Thick}(F\oplus M)\xrightarrow{\cong}{\textup{D}}_{\textup{Perf}}(\Sigma_{M})\quad\quad\text{and}\quad\quad\textup{thick}(F\oplus M)\xrightarrow{\cong}{\textup{D}_{\textup{perf}}}(\Sigma_{M})\ ,

intertwining the forgetful functor
{\textup{D}}(\Sigma_{M})\to\DGV
with
\Hom_{{\textup{D}}\textup{QCoh}(Y)}(F\oplus M,\cdot)
, and similarly

\textup{Thick}(M)\xrightarrow{\cong}{\textup{D}}_{\textup{Perf}}(\Sigma_{\infty})\quad\quad\text{and}\quad\quad\textup{thick}(M)\xrightarrow{\cong}{\textup{D}_{\textup{perf}}}(\Sigma_{\infty})\ ,

intertwining the forgetful functor
{\textup{D}}(\Sigma_{\infty})\to\DGV
with
\Hom_{{\textup{D}}\textup{QCoh}(Y)}(M,\cdot)
.

Proof.

As in the analogous statement for
F
, we apply the DG Morita theory of Keller
[
Kel06
]
recalled in Theorem
2.6
to the thick subcategory generated by the objects
F\oplus M
and
M
, respectively.
∎

Further, we let
I_{M}=I\cup\{\infty\}
and define

S_{\infty}=\Ext^{0}(M,M)\ \in{\textup{D}}_{\textup{Fd}}(\Sigma_{M})\quad\quad\textup{and}\quad\quad S_{M}=\bigoplus_{i\in I_{M}}S_{i}=S\oplus S_{\infty}\ \in{\textup{D}}_{\textup{Fd}}(\Sigma_{M})\ ,

as well as their natural graded enhancements. Note that the module structure on
S_{\infty}
factors through the natural projection
\Sigma_{M}\to\Sigma_{\infty}
, or equivalently is pulled back from a module
S_{\infty}\in{\textup{D}}_{\textup{Fd}}(\Sigma_{\infty})
, for which we use the same notation by abuse, and similarly for the graded variants.

Further, as in Section
3.3
, we can introduce corresponding Koszul dual graded algebras

\Lambda_{\infty}=\Hom_{\Sigma_{\infty}}(S_{\infty},S_{\infty})\quad\quad\text{and}\quad\quad\Lambda_{M}=\Hom_{\Sigma_{M}}(S_{M},S_{M})\ ,

as well as their I-adically complete, ungraded variants
\hat{\Lambda}_{\infty}
and
\hat{\Lambda}_{M}
. As in Equation
5.16
, we have induced presentations of
\hat{\Lambda}_{\infty}
and
\hat{\Lambda}_{M}
(and their graded variants) as quasi-free complete (or graded) DG associative algebras, with underlying cohomologically (and abstractly bi)graded associative algebras given by

\ .

We again let
S_{M}\in\hat{\Lambda}_{M}{\textup{-Mod}}
and similarly
S_{M}\in\Lambda_{M}{\textup{-Mod}}_{\mathbb{Z}}
denote the corresponding augmentation modules, and we make the following definition:

Definition 4.15
.

The derived category
{\textup{D}}_{\textup{Fr}}(\hat{\Lambda}_{M})
of finite rank (over
S_{M}
)
\hat{\Lambda}_{M}
modules is defined as the thick subcategory
{\textup{D}}_{\textup{Fr}}(\hat{\Lambda}_{M})=\textup{Thick}(S_{M})
generated by
S_{M}
, and similarly for the category of plain finite rank modules
\hat{\Lambda}_{M}{\textup{-Mod}}_{\textup{Fr}}=\textup{Filt}(S_{M})
. Their graded variants are defined similarly, as
{\textup{D}}_{\textup{fr}}(\Lambda_{M})=\textup{thick}(S_{M})
and
\Lambda_{M}{\textup{-Mod}}_{\textup{fr}}=\textup{filt}(S_{M})
.

We again have induced Koszul duality equivalences, which are the analogues for
\Sigma_{M}
and
\Sigma_{\infty}
of the equivalences relating
\Sigma
modules and
\Lambda
modules given in Corollary
3.10
:

Corollary 4.16
.

There are mutually inverse equivalences of triangulated categories

\displaystyle\Hom_{\Lambda_{M}}(S_{M},\cdot)

\displaystyle:\lx@xy@svg{\hbox{\raise 2.5pt\hbox{\kern 21.4688pt\hbox{\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\hbox{\vtop{\halign{\entry@#!@&&\entry@@#!@\cr&\crcr}}}\ignorespaces{\hbox{\kern-21.4688pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 3.0pt\raise-2.5pt\hbox{$\textstyle{{\textup{D}}_{\textup{fr}}(\Lambda_{\infty})\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}$}}}}}}}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces{}{\hbox{\lx@xy@droprule}}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces{\hbox{\kern 29.96013pt\raise 8.30276pt\hbox{{}\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 3.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise-1.75pt\hbox{$\scriptstyle{\cong}$}}}\kern 3.0pt}}}}}}\ignorespaces{\hbox{\kern 45.4688pt\raise 2.15277pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\lx@xy@tip{1}\lx@xy@tip{-1}}}}}}{\hbox{\lx@xy@droprule}}{\hbox{\lx@xy@droprule}}{\hbox{\kern 45.4688pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 3.0pt\raise-2.5pt\hbox{$\textstyle{\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces{\textup{D}_{\textup{perf}}}(\Sigma_{\infty})}$}}}}}}}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces{}{\hbox{\lx@xy@droprule}}\ignorespaces{\hbox{\kern 21.4688pt\raise-2.15277pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\lx@xy@tip{1}\lx@xy@tip{-1}}}}}}{\hbox{\lx@xy@droprule}}{\hbox{\lx@xy@droprule}}\ignorespaces}}}}\ignorespaces:(\cdot)\otimes_{\Sigma_{\infty}}S_{\infty}\quad\quad\ \ .

Proof.

Follows from the proof of Corollary
3.10
,
mutatis mutandis
.
∎

We now proceed to prove the generalization of Theorem
3.11
to the thick subcategory
\textup{Thick}(F\oplus M)
, and its graded variant. To begin, we note

Proposition 4.17
.

There exist functors

\displaystyle(\cdot)\otimes_{S_{M}}S

\displaystyle:{\textup{D}}_{\textup{Perf}}(\Sigma_{M})\to{\textup{D}}_{\textup{Fd}}(\Sigma)

\displaystyle(\cdot)\otimes_{S_{M}}S

\displaystyle:{\textup{D}_{\textup{perf}}}(\Sigma_{M})\to{\textup{D}}_{\textup{fd}}(\Sigma)

\displaystyle(\cdot)\otimes_{\hat{\Lambda}_{M}}\hat{\Lambda}

\displaystyle:{\textup{D}}_{\textup{Fr}}(\hat{\Lambda}_{M})\to{\textup{D}}_{\textup{Perf}}(\hat{\Lambda})

\displaystyle(\cdot)\otimes_{\Lambda_{M}}\Lambda

\displaystyle:{\textup{D}}_{\textup{fr}}(\Lambda_{M})\to{\textup{D}_{\textup{perf}}}(\Lambda)

.

Proof.

The codomain of the functors in the first line are as claimed, since
\Sigma_{M}\otimes_{S_{M}}S=\Hom(F,F\oplus M)
is finite dimensional over the base field, as
F
has compact support. The codomain of the functors on the second line are as claimed since we have
{\textup{D}}_{\textup{Fr}}(\hat{\Lambda}_{M})\subset{\textup{D}}_{\textup{Perf}}(\hat{\Lambda}_{M})
, and similarly for the graded variant, and the functors are clearly defined on the latter categories and preserve perfect complexes.
∎

In terms of these functors, the desired generalization of Theorem
3.11
is the following:

Theorem 4.18
.

The diagram of triangulated categories

(4.11)

\textstyle{\textup{Thick}(F,M)\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}
\scriptstyle{\subset}
\scriptstyle{\Hom_{\hat{Y}}(F\oplus M,\cdot)\otimes_{\Sigma_{M}}S_{M}}

To complete the proof, we will need the following lemma:

Lemma 4.19
.

The diagrams of triangulated categories

\textstyle{{\textup{D}}_{\textup{Perf}}(\Sigma_{M})\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}
\scriptstyle{(\cdot)^{N_{\Sigma_{M}}\circ\subset}}
\scriptstyle{(\cdot)\otimes_{S_{M}}S}
\textstyle{{\textup{D}}_{{\textup{Fr}}}(\Sigma_{M})\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}
\scriptstyle{(\cdot)\otimes_{S_{M}}S}
\textstyle{{\textup{D}}_{\textup{Fd}}(\Sigma)\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}
\scriptstyle{(\cdot)^{N_{\Sigma}}}
\textstyle{{\textup{D}}_{\textup{Fd}}(\Sigma)}

and

\textstyle{{\textup{D}_{\textup{perf}}}(\Sigma_{M})\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}
\scriptstyle{(\cdot)^{N_{\Sigma_{M}}\circ\subset}}
\scriptstyle{(\cdot)\otimes_{S_{M}}S}
\textstyle{{\textup{D}}_{{\textup{fr}}}(\Sigma_{M})\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}
\scriptstyle{(\cdot)\otimes_{S_{M}}S}
\textstyle{{\textup{D}}_{\textup{fd}}(\Sigma)\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}
\scriptstyle{(\cdot)^{N_{\Sigma}}}
\textstyle{{\textup{D}}_{\textup{fd}}(\Sigma)}

admit canonical commutativity data., where
(\cdot)^{N_{\Sigma_{M}}}:{\textup{D}}_{\textup{Fr}}(\Sigma_{M})\to{\textup{D}}_{\textup{Fr}}(\Sigma_{M})
denotes the Nakayama functor for
\Sigma_{M}
and similarly for
N_{\Sigma}
and their graded variants.

Proof.

First, note that we have the natural isomorphism

\displaystyle S\otimes_{S_{M}}\Sigma_{M}^{N_{\Sigma_{M}}}\otimes_{S_{M}}S

\displaystyle=S\otimes_{S_{M}}\Hom_{S_{M}}(\Sigma_{M},S_{M})\otimes_{S_{M}}S

\displaystyle\cong\Hom_{S_{M}}(\Sigma_{M},S)\otimes_{S_{M}}S

\displaystyle\cong\Hom_{S_{M}}(\Hom(F,F\oplus M),S)\otimes_{S_{M}}S

\displaystyle\cong\Hom_{S_{M}}(\Hom(F,F),S)

\displaystyle\cong\Sigma^{N_{\Sigma}}

.

Now, it suffices to check the result on the generator
\Sigma_{M}
of
{\textup{D}}_{\textup{Perf}}(\Sigma_{M})
; we have

\displaystyle\Sigma_{M}\otimes_{S_{M}}S\otimes_{\Sigma}\Sigma^{N_{\Sigma}}

\displaystyle=\Sigma_{M}\otimes_{S_{M}}S\otimes_{\Sigma}\left(S\otimes_{S_{M}}\Sigma_{M}^{N_{\Sigma_{M}}}\otimes_{S_{M}}S\right)

\displaystyle\cong S\otimes_{S_{M}}\Sigma_{M}\otimes_{S_{M}}S\otimes_{\Sigma}\left(\Sigma_{M}^{N_{\Sigma_{M}}}\otimes_{S_{M}}S\right)

\displaystyle\cong\Sigma_{M}^{N_{\Sigma_{M}}}\otimes_{S_{M}}S

,

where the first equality follows from the preceding natural isomorphism.
∎

Proof.

(of Theorem
4.18
)
Note that we have already established the existence of the mutually inverse triangle equivalences in the bottom rows of the diagram in Theorem
3.11
, and those in the top rows in Corollaries
4.14
and
4.16
. Thus, it remains to check commutativity, which we now prove for the rightmost and outer squares, as this is sufficient:

For the rightmost squares, applying the preceding lemma, we have the natural isomorphism

\displaystyle\Hom_{\Sigma}(S,(\Hom_{\hat{\Lambda}_{M}}(S_{M},\cdot)\otimes_{S_{M}}S)^{N_{\Sigma}})

\displaystyle\cong\Hom_{\Sigma}(S,(\Hom_{\hat{\Lambda}_{M}}(S_{M},\cdot)^{N_{\Sigma_{M}}}\otimes_{S_{M}}S))

\displaystyle\cong\Hom_{\Sigma}(S,(\cdot)\otimes_{\hat{\Lambda}_{M}}S_{M}\otimes_{S_{M}}S)

\displaystyle\cong\Hom_{\Sigma}(S,(\cdot)\otimes_{\hat{\Lambda}_{M}}\hat{\Lambda}\otimes_{\hat{\Lambda}}S)

\displaystyle\cong(\cdot)\otimes_{\hat{\Lambda}_{M}}\hat{\Lambda}

,

as desired, and similarly for the graded case. Commutativity of the outer squares follows from the proof of Theorem
3.11
, noting we have the natural isomorphism

\Hom_{\hat{Y}}(F\oplus M,\cdot)\otimes_{S_{M}}S\cong\Hom_{\hat{Y}}(F,\cdot)\ ,

and similarly for the graded case.
∎

Proof.

∎

Moreover, we have the following induced equivalences of the natural hearts of these categories:

Corollary 4.22
.

induces mutually inverse equivalences of mixed categories
